title: Introduction to Pricing & Selling
subtitle: Work out what your product really costs, set a price that pays you a real profit, and sell it with calm confidence.
description: A practical course for women who make or sell products or services. You will calculate your true cost including your own time, set prices using cost-plus, competitor and value-based methods, understand markup, margin and discounts, handle price objections, and keep daily sales records that show your real profit.
outcomes: Calculate the true cost per item or per job, including materials, labour, overhead and waste
Set a price using cost-plus, competitor and value-based pricing, and explain the difference between markup and margin
Work out how a discount changes profit and design offers that protect your margin
Lead a selling conversation and respond to price objections without going below cost
Keep a daily sales book and use margin and break-even figures to make decisions
Produce a one-page pricing sheet and a 90-day pricing review plan
audience: Women in Nigeria and across Africa who sell, or plan to sell, a product or service and want to stop guessing their prices.
tools: A notebook and pen, or a free spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets
Receipts or notes of what you spend on inputs
WhatsApp (the WhatsApp Business app is helpful but optional)
One product or service of your own to price

modules.title: Foundations: know your true cost
modules.overview: Understand the difference between cost, price and profit, then calculate the true cost of one product or service, including your own time and overheads. You will also set up simple records and protect yourself from payment scams before you start changing prices.

lessons.title: Cost, price and profit: why so many sellers undercharge
objectives: Explain the difference between cost, price and profit in plain words
Identify the three common pricing mistakes small sellers make
Describe the price floor, the market range and the value ceiling
Write down your own product and current price as a starting point

blocks.text: Every sale has three numbers behind it. **Cost** is the money (and time) it takes you to make or buy the thing you sell. **Price** is what the customer pays you. **Profit** is what is left when you take cost away from price. If a pack of chin chin costs you ₦550 to make and you sell it for ₦800, your profit on that pack is ₦250. If you sell it for ₦500, you are not making a small profit: you are losing ₦50 on every pack, even if your purse feels full at the end of the day.

That last point surprises many people. Money coming in is called **revenue** or sales. Revenue is not profit. A woman can sell ₦40,000 of goods in a week and still be poorer than when she started, because the cost of those goods was higher than she realised. This course is about seeing your real numbers clearly, choosing a price on purpose, and then selling at that price with calm confidence.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A woman working out figures on a large calculator
blocks.caption: Before you choose a price, you need to know what each item really costs you.

blocks.text: Three mistakes that keep sellers poor

items: **Counting only materials.** Many sellers add up flour, sugar and oil, then stop. They forget packaging, transport to market, gas, phone data for WhatsApp orders, and most of all, their own hours of work.

**Copying the next seller's price.** The woman beside you may buy in bulk, use cheaper inputs, have no shop rent, or simply be losing money without knowing it. Her price tells you about the market, not about your cost.

**Never reviewing the price.** In Nigeria the cost of inputs such as flour, cooking gas and transport can change quickly. A price that gave a good profit six months ago can quietly turn into a loss if you never recalculate.

blocks.text: You will learn to fix each of these. Module 1 helps you find your true cost. Module 2 shows you how to turn that cost into a price using three methods: cost-plus, competitor-based and value-based pricing, and how discounts affect your profit. Module 3 is about the selling conversation, objections and daily records. Module 4 brings it together into a pricing sheet and a 90-day review plan.
The three prices every product has

It helps to picture three levels for any product or service. The first is your **price floor**: your true cost per item. Below this you lose money on every sale. The second is the **market range**: what similar products sell for around you, from the cheapest to the most expensive. The third is the **value ceiling**: the highest amount a customer would happily pay because of what your product does for them, such as saving time, looking good at an event, or tasting fresher than the rest.

blocks.title: Where a good price sits
items: Value ceiling: what buyers gladly pay
Market range: what others charge
Price floor: your true cost
blocks.caption: A healthy price sits above your floor, inside or near the market range, and below what your best customers believe it is worth.

blocks.text: Your job is to choose a price that is **always above the floor**, makes sense against the market range, and moves closer to the value ceiling as your quality, reputation and service improve. A seller who only looks at the floor may price too low. A seller who only looks at competitors may price below her own cost. A seller who only dreams about value may price so high that no one buys. You need all three views.

blocks.title: Worked example: the busy seller who was losing money
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi sells small packs of chin chin to offices in Enugu. She charges ₦500 a pack because that is what another seller charges. All figures here are approximate and only for illustration.
steps: She adds up one batch: ingredients and gas about ₦13,000, packaging about ₦2,000, transport and data about ₦2,000.
That is ₦17,000 for 40 packs, or ₦425 a pack. She thinks she makes ₦75 profit on each one.
Then she counts her time: about 5 hours of mixing, cutting, frying and packing. She values her time at about ₦1,000 an hour, so ₦5,000 per batch.
Her true cost is ₦22,000 for 40 packs, which is ₦550 a pack.
blocks.result: At ₦500 a pack she is giving away ₦50 of her labour on every sale. She is not running a business yet; she is subsidising her customers. Lesson 2 shows how to do this calculation step by step.

blocks.title: Why your time counts
blocks.text: If you do not pay yourself for your hours, the business looks profitable only because you are working for free. One day you may want to hire help, take a rest week or grow. If your price never included labour, you will not be able to afford any of these.
What a good price does for you

items: It covers every cost, including your time, so the business can keep going.
It leaves a profit you can save, reinvest in stock, or use to grow.
It gives you room to offer a planned discount without falling below cost.
It sends a message about quality: a price far below everyone else can make buyers suspicious.

blocks.title: Start with one product
blocks.text: Do not try to price everything at once. Pick the one product or service you sell most often, or plan to sell first. You will use it in every activity in this course, so by the end you will have a fully worked price for it.

takeaways: Revenue is money coming in; profit is what remains after all costs.
Count materials, packaging, overhead and your own time, not only ingredients.
A competitor's price shows the market, not your cost.
Every product has a floor (cost), a market range and a value ceiling.
Review prices regularly because input costs change.

activity.title: Write your starting point
steps: Choose one product or service you sell or plan to sell.
Write down its current price, or the price you planned to charge.
Write how you chose that price: guess, copied someone, or calculated.
List every cost you can think of for one item or one job, even if you do not know the amounts yet.
Ask two buyers or friends what they would expect to pay for it and note their answers.
activity.evidence: A page in your notebook (or a phone note) titled 'My starting price' with the product, price, how it was chosen and your cost list.

lessons.title: Finding your true cost per item
objectives: Separate direct costs, labour and overhead
Set a fair hourly rate for your own labour
Calculate the true cost of one unit from a batch
Calculate the true cost of a service job

blocks.text: Your true cost is the total of everything it takes to produce one item or deliver one job. To find it, you sort your costs into three groups, add them for a whole batch (or a whole month), and then divide by the number of items you make. This lesson walks you through each group and two full examples, one for a product and one for a service.
Group 1: direct costs (materials and packaging)

**Direct costs** are things that go into, or onto, the product. If you make one more item, you use more of them. For food this is ingredients, cooking gas or charcoal, and packaging such as nylon, labels and containers. For a tailor it is thread, lining, zips, buttons and interfacing. For a reseller of shoes or bags it is the price you paid the wholesaler plus the cost of bringing the goods home.

Use what you actually paid, from your last receipts or market trip, not what you hope to pay. If you buy a 10 kg bag of flour and use 2 kg per batch, only count one fifth of the bag's price in each batch.
Group 2: your labour

**Labour** is the time you, and anyone who helps you, spend making and selling. Count shopping for inputs, preparing, producing, packing and delivering. To put a value on your hour, ask: what could I reasonably earn doing similar work for someone else? For example, if similar daily work in your area pays about ₦8,000 for an 8-hour day, your hour is worth about ₦1,000. If someone helps you and you pay them, their pay goes here too.

blocks.title: Labour is a cost, not your profit
blocks.text: Paying yourself for your hours is your wage. Profit is extra money the business earns on top of everyone's wages. Keeping the two separate tells you whether the business itself is healthy.
Group 3: overhead

**Overhead** is the cost of running the business that does not belong to one single item: stall or shop rent, market levy, electricity or generator fuel, phone data for WhatsApp orders, transport to market, POS charges and equipment wear. Add these up for a month, then share them across everything you make in that month. If your overhead is ₦20,000 a month and you make 400 packs, each pack carries ₦50 of overhead.

blocks.name: ledger
blocks.alt: A ledger book for recording costs
blocks.caption: Write every cost in one place so nothing is forgotten when you add up.

blocks.title: From costs to cost per item
items: Direct costs per batch
Add labour per batch
Add overhead share
Divide by items made
True cost per item
blocks.caption: Add the three cost groups for one batch, then divide by the number of good items the batch produced.

blocks.title: Worked example: true cost of a pack of chin chin
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi makes chin chin in batches of 40 packs. All naira figures are approximate and will differ by city and season.
steps: Direct costs per batch: flour ₦3,000, sugar ₦1,200, margarine ₦2,500, eggs ₦1,500, milk and nutmeg ₦800, frying oil ₦3,000, cooking gas ₦1,000. Total ₦13,000.
Packaging: 40 nylon packs with labels at about ₦50 each is ₦2,000.
Labour: 5 hours at ₦1,000 an hour is ₦5,000.
Overhead share: transport to deliver ₦1,500 plus phone data ₦500 is ₦2,000.
Cost per pack: ₦22,000 divided by 40 = ₦550.
blocks.result: ₦550 is Ngozi's price floor. Any price below ₦550 means she is losing money, even if it does not feel like it.

blocks.title: Worked example: true cost of a sewing job
blocks.context: For example, Amaka sews an Ankara gown when the customer brings her own fabric. Figures are approximate.
steps: Direct costs: lining ₦2,000, zip and thread ₦1,000, interfacing ₦500. Total ₦3,500.
Labour: cutting, sewing and a fitting take about 6 hours at ₦1,000 an hour, so ₦6,000.
Overhead: her monthly overhead (generator fuel, machine servicing, data) is about ₦30,000 and she completes about 20 gowns a month, so ₦1,500 per gown.
blocks.result: Amaka should not accept a gown job below ₦11,000. Module 2 shows how she sets a price above this floor.

blocks.title: Allow for waste
blocks.text: Some items break, burn, expire or are given as samples. If 2 of every 40 packs are usually spoiled or tasted, divide the batch cost by 38, not 40. Ignoring waste makes your cost look lower than it really is.
A simple cost sheet

head: Cost group
What to include
Where to find the number
rows: Ingredients, materials, packaging, goods bought for resale
Your hours and any helper's pay
Time yourself for one full batch
Rent, levy, fuel, data, transport, POS charges
Last month's spending, divided by items made
Count over two or three batches

blocks.text: Keep this sheet. Every time an input price changes, update the line and recalculate. It takes five minutes and protects your profit.

takeaways: True cost = direct costs + labour + overhead share, divided by good items made.
Value your hour at what similar work pays locally.
Spread monthly overhead across everything you make that month.
Allow for waste and samples.
Your true cost per item is your price floor.

activity.title: Calculate your true cost
steps: Write all direct costs for one batch or one job, using real receipts.
Time yourself for one full batch or job and multiply by your hourly rate.
Add up last month's overhead and divide by the number of items you made.
Add the three totals and divide by the number of good items.
Compare this true cost with your current price from Lesson 1.
activity.evidence: A completed cost sheet showing each cost group, the batch total and the cost per item.

lessons.title: Getting ready: business money, records and payment safety
objectives: Separate business money from personal money
Set up a simple notebook or phone sheet for prices and sales
Recognise common payment scams such as fake transfer alerts
Confirm payments safely before releasing goods

blocks.text: Before you change any price, set up three habits that make every later lesson easier: keep business money apart from household money, write things down, and protect yourself from payment fraud. None of these needs a computer. A notebook, a pen and your phone are enough.

blocks.name: wallet
blocks.alt: A wallet with cash and cards
blocks.caption: Keep business money in its own place so you can see what the business really earns.

blocks.text: Habit 1: separate business money

If sales money goes into the same purse or account as school fees and food money, you can never tell whether the business is making a profit. A simple fix is to open a separate account or wallet just for the business. Many sellers use a second account with their bank, or a business account with a provider such as Moniepoint, Opay or Paystack, so that every customer transfer lands in one place.

Then pay yourself on purpose. For example, decide that every Friday you move a fixed amount from the business account to your personal account as your wage. Whatever stays in the business account is for restocking and profit. This one habit makes your labour cost real.
Habit 2: write things down

You will need three short records: your **cost sheet** (from Lesson 2), a **price list** (what you charge for each item), and a **daily sales book** (what you sold each day). A notebook works well. If you prefer your phone, a free spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets lets you add up columns automatically. Module 3 shows the sales book in detail.

head: Record
What it shows
How often to update
rows: Your price for each product or service

blocks.text: Keep your receipts too. Put market receipts, wholesaler invoices and transport notes in one envelope or snap a photo of each with your phone. When you sit down to recalculate your cost, the real numbers are right there, and you are not relying on memory. If a supplier does not give receipts, write the amount and date in your notebook as soon as you pay.

Also check what each payment method costs you. Some POS operators and payment providers charge a small fee on each transaction, and some customers ask you to pay for delivery or packaging separately. Find out the actual charges on the method you use and include them in your overhead, so that a sale paid by card or transfer does not quietly earn you less than a cash sale.
Habit 3: protect every payment

Transfers have made selling easier, but they have also brought scams. One of the most common in Nigeria is the **fake alert**: a buyer shows you a screenshot, or a fake SMS arrives, saying money has been sent, but no money has entered your account. Others pretend to overpay and ask for a refund of the difference. Some send a message that looks like it is from your bank and ask for your PIN or a code.

blocks.title: Before you release goods
items: Open your bank or wallet app
See the credit in your balance
Check amount and sender name
Never share PIN or OTP
Then hand over the goods
blocks.caption: A screenshot or SMS is not proof of payment; only money in your balance is.

blocks.title: Rules that keep you safe
blocks.text: Only trust money you can see in your account balance inside your banking or wallet app. Never give anyone your PIN, password or one-time code (OTP), including people claiming to be from your bank. Do not refund an 'overpayment' until the full amount has truly arrived, and refund to the same account it came from. If a deal feels rushed, slow down.

blocks.title: Worked example: the Saturday rush
blocks.context: For example, Halima sells fabric at a busy market in Kano. On a Saturday a buyer picks ₦45,000 of fabric and says he has transferred the money. He shows a screenshot and is in a hurry. Figures are approximate.
steps: Halima politely says, 'Thank you, let me just confirm it on my phone.'
She opens her bank app. Her balance has not changed.
She waits two minutes and refreshes. Still nothing.
She says, 'Sometimes transfers delay. You can wait, or pay by POS or cash.' She keeps the fabric folded beside her.
The buyer leaves without paying.
blocks.result: Halima loses nothing. A screenshot is easy to fake; her real balance is not. Saying 'let me confirm' calmly is normal business, not rudeness.

blocks.text: Your readiness check

items: Do you have one product or service you will use throughout this course?
Do you know its true cost, or do you have the receipts to calculate it?
Do you have a place to keep business money separate?
Do you have a notebook or phone sheet for records?
Do you feel comfortable saying your price out loud? If not, that is normal; Module 3 will help.

blocks.title: Think back to a real sale
blocks.text: Remember one recent sale or a sale you lost. What did the customer say about the price? What did you say? Write it down. You will use this real moment later when you practise objections.

takeaways: Keep business money separate and pay yourself a planned wage.
Three records: cost sheet, price list, daily sales book.
A screenshot or SMS is not proof of payment.
Never share your PIN, password or OTP.
Confirm money in your balance before releasing goods.

activity.title: Set up your money and records
steps: Choose or open a separate account or wallet for business money.
Decide how much and how often you will pay yourself.
Prepare a notebook or phone sheet with three sections: costs, price list, daily sales.
Write your own payment-safety rule on the first page.
Write down one recent sales conversation and what was said about price.
activity.evidence: A photo of your record book's first page showing the three sections and your payment-safety rule.

quiz.q: Ngozi sells a pack for ₦500. Her true cost per pack, including her labour, is ₦550. What is happening on each sale?
quiz.explain: Profit = price minus true cost = ₦500 − ₦550 = −₦50. Money comes in, but it is less than the cost of making the pack.

quiz.q: Which of these is an overhead cost for a food seller?
quiz.explain: Overhead is a running cost that is not tied to a single item, like rent or a market levy. Flour, eggs and packs are direct costs.

quiz.q: A batch costs ₦18,000 in total and makes 40 items, but 4 are usually spoiled. What is the true cost per good item?
quiz.explain: Divide by the good items only: ₦18,000 ÷ 36 = ₦500. Dividing by 40 would hide the cost of waste.

quiz.q: A buyer shows a screenshot of a ₦30,000 transfer, but your balance has not changed. What should you do?
options: Release the goods because the screenshot is proof
Wait, refresh your app, and offer POS or cash if the money has not arrived
Ask the buyer for your OTP to check
quiz.explain: Only money visible in your balance is proof. Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked.

quiz.q: Why should your own labour be included in your cost?
options: So the business can afford rest, help or growth, and you can see if it is truly profitable
To make prices look higher than competitors
quiz.explain: Without labour in the cost, the business only looks profitable because you work for free.

quiz.q: Amaka's monthly overhead is ₦30,000 and she sews 20 gowns a month. How much overhead should each gown carry?
quiz.explain: ₦30,000 ÷ 20 gowns = ₦1,500 per gown.

modules.title: Guided practice: from cost to the right price
modules.overview: Turn your true cost into a price using cost-plus pricing, check it against competitors and the value you offer, and learn exactly how markup, margin and discounts change your profit. Every method is practised with worked naira examples.

lessons.title: Cost-plus pricing and the markup versus margin trap
objectives: Set a price using cost-plus pricing
Calculate markup and margin from the same cost and price
Work out the price needed for a target margin
Avoid the common mistake of confusing markup with margin

blocks.text: The simplest way to turn a cost into a price is **cost-plus pricing**: start from your true cost per item and add a chosen percentage on top. It is easy, it guarantees you never price below cost, and it is the right first step for almost every small seller. Its weakness is that it ignores what customers will pay, which is why Lesson 2 adds the market view. Here we master the arithmetic, because one small confusion costs sellers a lot of money.
Markup and margin: same profit, two percentages
Suppose a pack costs you ₦550 and you sell it for ₦800. Your profit is ₦250. You can describe that ₦250 in two ways:

items: **Markup** compares profit with **cost**: ₦250 ÷ ₦550 = 0.455, so a markup of about 45%.
**Margin** compares profit with **price**: ₦250 ÷ ₦800 = 0.3125, so a margin of about 31%.

blocks.text: Both are correct. They are just measured against different bases. Markup is always the bigger number because cost is smaller than price. Accountants and business advisers usually talk about margin; many traders in the market think in markup. Trouble starts when you mix them up.

blocks.title: Markup versus margin
items: Markup: profit over cost
Margin: profit over price
blocks.caption: The same ₦250 profit is a 45% markup but only a 31% margin, because the bases are different.
right: Shows share of each sale kept

blocks.text: The two formulas you need

items: To price with a **markup**: price = cost × (1 + markup). For a 50% markup on ₦550: ₦550 × 1.5 = ₦825.
To price with a **target margin**: price = cost ÷ (1 − margin). For a 40% margin on ₦550: ₦550 ÷ 0.6 = ₦916.67.
To check what you have: markup = profit ÷ cost, and margin = profit ÷ price.
Round your final price to a figure that is easy to pay and give change for, such as ₦800, ₦900 or ₦1,000, and recheck the margin after rounding.

blocks.title: The common trap
blocks.text: If you want to keep 30% of every sale as profit (a 30% margin) but you simply add 30% to cost, you get ₦550 × 1.3 = ₦715. Your real margin is only ₦165 ÷ ₦715 = 23%. To truly keep 30%, price = ₦550 ÷ 0.7 = ₦785.71, so about ₦790 or ₦800.

blocks.name: abacus
blocks.caption: Markup and margin are simple division, but you must divide by the right number.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi chooses her price
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi's true cost per pack of chin chin is ₦550 (from Module 1). She wants a margin of about 30%. Figures are approximate.
steps: She rounds up to ₦800 because it is easy to pay by cash or transfer.
Check profit: ₦800 − ₦550 = ₦250 per pack.
Check margin: ₦250 ÷ ₦800 = 31%. Check markup: ₦250 ÷ ₦550 = 45%.
If she sells 200 packs in a month, profit after paying herself is 200 × ₦250 = ₦50,000.
blocks.result: ₦800 covers every cost including her wage and leaves a clear profit. Next she checks it against what other sellers charge.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing a resold item
blocks.context: For example, Chioma buys ladies' sandals from a wholesaler and resells them to customers on WhatsApp in Port Harcourt. Figures are approximate.
steps: She pays ₦7,000 a pair when she buys 20 pairs.
Her transport to and from the wholesale market is ₦10,000 for the trip, which is ₦500 a pair.
Her monthly overhead (data, nylon bags, delivery rider top-ups) works out at about ₦500 a pair. Her time sourcing, posting and replying adds about ₦1,000 a pair.
For a 35% margin: ₦9,000 ÷ 0.65 = ₦13,846. She rounds to ₦14,000. Profit ₦5,000, margin 36%.
blocks.result: Many resellers price at 'what I bought it for plus a little'. Chioma's method shows that transport, overhead and time are a large part of a resold item's real cost.

blocks.text: Notice that in both examples the seller worked from cost to price, then rounded. Rounding up a little is usually safe; rounding down can eat your margin, so always recheck the profit after rounding. Keep your workings in your notebook so you can repeat them quickly when costs change.
How much markup is normal?

There is no single correct percentage. It depends on how fast items sell, how much risk you carry and how much skill is involved. Fast-moving goods that you simply buy and resell often carry a lower markup and make money through volume. Handmade items, services and goods that spoil or go out of fashion usually need a higher markup to cover time, waste and unsold stock. Rather than copying a 'standard' percentage, start with your true cost, test a margin you can live with, and compare it with the market in the next lesson.

blocks.title: Write both numbers on your price list
blocks.text: Next to each item, write the cost, the price, the markup and the margin. Seeing the margin every day stops you giving away more discount than the item can carry.

takeaways: Cost-plus: price = cost × (1 + markup).
Target margin: price = cost ÷ (1 − margin).
Markup is profit over cost; margin is profit over price.
Adding 30% to cost does not give a 30% margin.
Round to an easy price, then recheck the margin.

activity.title: Price your product with cost-plus
steps: Take your true cost per item from Module 1.
Calculate prices at 25%, 50% and 100% markup.
Calculate the price for a 30% and a 40% margin.
Choose one rounded price and write its profit, markup and margin.
Explain in one sentence why you chose that margin.

lessons.title: Checking the market: competitor and value-based pricing
objectives: Run a simple competitor price survey
Compare prices fairly using price per unit of size or weight
Identify the value your product gives customers
Set a value-based price above cost and within reason

blocks.text: Cost-plus pricing tells you the lowest price you can accept. It does not tell you what buyers will pay. Two more methods fill that gap. **Competitor-based pricing** looks at what similar sellers charge. **Value-based pricing** looks at what your product is worth to the customer. Good sellers use all three together: cost sets the floor, competitors show the range, value tells you where in the range, or above it, you belong.
Step 1: survey the market

items: List five to eight sellers your customers could buy from instead of you: in your market, on WhatsApp status, on Instagram, or in nearby shops.
Record each seller's price, size or quantity, and anything special (branding, delivery, freshness, location).
Compare like with like. Divide the price by the size to get the price per 100 g, per litre, or per piece.
Note the lowest, the middle and the highest price per unit. That is your market range.
Mark where your own price sits in that range.

blocks.title: Worked example: comparing chin chin prices fairly
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi's 200 g pack is priced at ₦800. She checks four other sellers near her customers' offices. Figures are approximate.
steps: Seller A: 150 g for ₦600, which is ₦400 per 100 g.
Seller B: 250 g for ₦900, which is ₦360 per 100 g.
Seller C: 200 g in a branded tub for ₦1,200, which is ₦600 per 100 g.
Seller D: 100 g for ₦500, which is ₦500 per 100 g.
Ngozi: 200 g for ₦800, which is ₦400 per 100 g.
blocks.result: Ngozi is in the lower middle of a range from ₦360 to ₦600 per 100 g. She is not too expensive. With better packaging she could move toward Seller C's level.

blocks.title: Price and value positions
items: Overpriced: high price, low value
Premium: high price, high value
Cheap: low price, low value
Bargain: low price, high value
blocks.caption: Aim for bargain or premium; a high price with low perceived value loses customers, and a low price with low value earns little.

blocks.text: Step 2: find your value

Value is what the customer gains, not what you put in. Ask yourself: what problem does my product solve, and what would the buyer lose if they did not buy from me? Common sources of value include **convenience** (delivery to the office, ready on time), **quality** (fresher, neater stitching, longer lasting), **reliability** (you always deliver what you promise), **personal service** (fitting, advice, follow-up) and **trust** (clean preparation, clear labels, NAFDAC registration where it is required for your product).

items: Ask three regular customers why they buy from you. Their words are your value.
Notice what customers praise or complain about in other sellers' reviews and comments.
List the extras you give that others do not, such as free delivery within an area or a quick adjustment after fitting.

blocks.title: Worked example: a value-based price for a sewing job
blocks.context: For example, Amaka sews Ankara gowns. Her true cost is ₦11,000 per gown (Module 1). Local tailors charge roughly ₦12,000 to ₦25,000. Figures are approximate.
steps: Cost floor: ₦11,000. A 30% margin would give ₦11,000 ÷ 0.7 = about ₦15,700.
Her value: a proper fitting, delivery in 3 days when many tailors take 2 weeks, and one free adjustment.
Customers who need an outfit for a wedding on Saturday value speed highly.
She sets her standard price at ₦18,000 and a rush price (48 hours) at ₦22,000.
Check: at ₦18,000 profit is ₦7,000 and margin is ₦7,000 ÷ ₦18,000 = 39%.
blocks.result: Amaka's price is above cost, inside the market range, and justified by real value she can explain to every customer.

blocks.title: Prices must still be honest
blocks.text: Value-based pricing means charging for real benefits you deliver. It never means exaggerating quality, inventing claims, or charging one customer far more for the same thing just because she looks rich. That damages trust quickly.

blocks.name: window-shopping
blocks.alt: A shopper comparing items in shop windows
blocks.caption: Your customers compare prices too, so you should know the market before they ask.

blocks.text: Putting the three methods together

head: Method
Question it answers
Ngozi's answer
rows: What is the lowest safe price?
What do others charge for the same size?
What is it worth to my buyer?
Fresh, delivered to office, could justify more with better packaging

blocks.text: Be careful about racing to the bottom. If a competitor is much cheaper, find out why before you react: smaller size, lower quality inputs, no labour counted, or a different customer group. Matching a price you cannot afford only moves you from making a profit to making a loss. Often the better answer is to stay at your price and explain your difference clearly, or to offer a smaller, cheaper size for price-sensitive buyers.

If your cost-plus price is far above the whole market range, either your costs are too high (look for cheaper inputs, bulk buying or less waste), or you must clearly offer extra value. If your price is far below the range, you may be leaving profit on the table.

takeaways: Cost sets the floor; competitors show the range; value places you in it.
Compare price per 100 g, per litre or per piece, not just the sticker price.
Value comes from convenience, quality, reliability, service and trust.
Charge for real benefits only; never exaggerate.
If cost is above the market, cut costs or add clear value.

activity.title: Run your own market check
steps: List five competitors for your product or service.
Record their price and size, and calculate price per unit.
Write your market range: lowest, middle, highest.
Ask three customers what they value most about buying from you.
Decide whether to keep, raise or lower your price, and why.
activity.evidence: A market survey table with five competitors, prices per unit, your position, and three customer quotes about value.

lessons.title: Discounts and their real effect on profit
objectives: Calculate the profit lost when you give a discount
Work out how many extra sales a discount needs to break even
Design a bulk or loyalty offer that protects your margin
Decide when to say no to a discount request

blocks.text: A discount feels small to the customer, but it comes straight out of your profit, not out of your cost. That is why a 10% price cut can wipe out a third or more of what you earn on each item. Before you give any discount, you should know exactly what it costs you.
Why a small discount bites hard

Take Ngozi's pack again: price ₦800, true cost ₦550, profit ₦250. If she gives 10% off, the price falls by ₦80 to ₦720. Her cost does not change, so her profit falls from ₦250 to ₦170. The customer saved 10%, but Ngozi lost 32% of her profit on that pack.

head: Discount
New price
Profit per pack
Profit lost
Extra sales needed to earn the same

blocks.text: The extra-sales rule

To earn the same total profit after a discount, divide the old profit per item by the new profit per item. That tells you how many times more items you must sell. At 10% off: ₦250 ÷ ₦170 = 1.47. So if Ngozi normally sells 100 packs a week, she must sell about 147 packs at the discounted price just to stand still. At 20% off she would need about 278 packs. Ask yourself honestly: will the discount really bring that many more buyers?

blocks.title: Before you agree to a discount
items: Know cost and profit per item
Calculate new profit
Divide old by new profit
Compare with realistic extra sales
Agree, adjust or decline
blocks.caption: A quick calculation before every discount stops you trading hard for less money.

blocks.title: Worked example: a bulk order from an office
blocks.context: For example, an office manager asks Ngozi for 30 packs every Friday and wants a discount. Figures are approximate.
steps: Normally each pack carries about ₦50 of delivery and data overhead because she delivers small orders separately.
With one delivery for 30 packs, her overhead per pack drops to about ₦20, so her true cost falls from ₦550 to about ₦520.
She offers ₦750 per pack for orders of 30 or more.
Profit per pack: ₦750 − ₦520 = ₦230. On 30 packs that is ₦6,900 every Friday.
Margin check: ₦230 ÷ ₦750 = 31%, almost the same as her normal margin.
blocks.result: This is a good discount: it is paid for by a real cost saving and guaranteed volume, not by her own profit.

blocks.text: Better ways to say 'special offer'

items: **Add value instead of cutting price.** 'Buy 10, get 1 free' sounds generous. On 10 packs at ₦800 she receives ₦8,000; the 11 packs cost her 11 × ₦550 = ₦6,050; profit ₦1,950. A 10% discount on 10 packs gives ₦7,200 minus ₦5,500 = only ₦1,700. The free item costs her its cost, not its price.
**Discount for a reason you control:** bulk quantity, early payment, collection instead of delivery, or a slow day of the week.
**Set a time limit** such as 'this weekend only', so the lower price does not become the new normal.
**Bundle** a slow item with a popular one rather than cutting the popular item's price.

blocks.name: label
blocks.caption: Every discount on the label comes straight out of your profit, so plan it on paper first.

blocks.title: Never discount below your floor
blocks.text: If a discount takes your price under your true cost, every extra sale makes you poorer. It is better to lose that one sale politely than to train customers to expect a loss-making price.

blocks.title: Decide your limits before the customer asks
blocks.text: Write your normal price, your best bulk price and your walk-away price for each item. In a busy moment, you will not have time to calculate, and a written limit stops you agreeing to something you regret.
The opposite also works: small price rises

The extra-sales rule works in reverse. If Ngozi raises her price by 10%, from ₦800 to ₦880, her profit per pack rises from ₦250 to ₦330. Divide the old profit by the new: ₦250 ÷ ₦330 = 0.76. She could sell about 24% fewer packs and still earn the same total profit, with less work and fewer ingredients. That does not mean every price rise is wise, but it shows why a careful increase is often less risky than sellers fear, and why a discount is often more costly than it looks.

In open markets where bargaining is expected, think in naira, not percentages. Know how many naira of profit each item carries, decide how many of those naira you are willing to give up, and stop there. A customer who bargains you down from ₦800 to ₦700 has taken ₦100 of your ₦250 profit, which is 40% of it.

Finally, watch what discounts teach your customers. If you cut prices every time someone hesitates, buyers learn to hesitate. If you discount only for clear reasons, they learn that your price is fair and that the way to pay less is to buy more or commit regularly.

takeaways: A discount comes out of profit, not cost.
Extra sales needed = old profit per item ÷ new profit per item.
Good discounts are paid for by real savings or guaranteed volume.
Free items cost you their cost, so 'buy 10 get 1' can beat 10% off.
Write your walk-away price and never go below your floor.

activity.title: Test a discount on paper
steps: Write your price, true cost and profit per item.
Calculate the new profit at 5%, 10% and 20% off.
Use the extra-sales rule to see how many more you would need to sell.
Design one offer that protects your margin (bulk, bundle or free item).
Write your walk-away price for the item.
activity.evidence: A discount sheet showing the three discount calculations, your chosen offer with its profit, and your walk-away price.

quiz.q: An item costs ₦1,000 and sells for ₦1,500. What are the markup and the margin?
Bisi's true cost is ₦2,000 and she wants a 50% margin. What price should she charge?
quiz.explain: Price = cost ÷ (1 − margin) = ₦2,000 ÷ 0.5 = ₦4,000. Adding 50% to cost (₦3,000) would give only a 33% margin.

quiz.q: Seller A sells 500 ml of zobo for ₦400; Seller B sells 1 litre for ₦700. Which is cheaper per litre?
quiz.explain: Seller A is ₦800 per litre (₦400 × 2). Seller B is ₦700 per litre, so B is cheaper per litre.

quiz.q: Price ₦1,000, cost ₦600. A customer wants 10% off. How much profit is left on that item?
quiz.explain: New price ₦900 minus cost ₦600 = ₦300. Profit fell by a quarter for a 10% discount.

quiz.q: Using the same item (profit ₦400 normally, ₦300 after the discount), how many times more items must she sell to earn the same total profit?
quiz.explain: Old profit ÷ new profit = ₦400 ÷ ₦300 = 1.33, so about a third more sales.

quiz.q: Which discount is most likely to protect a seller's profit?
options: A lower price for a large regular order that saves delivery costs
Cutting the price below cost to beat a competitor
quiz.explain: A bulk price backed by a real cost saving and guaranteed volume keeps the margin healthy.

modules.title: Selling with confidence and keeping evidence
modules.overview: Learn a simple five-stage selling conversation, practise answering price objections and bargaining without going below your floor, and keep a daily sales book that shows your real profit, margin and break-even point.

lessons.title: The selling conversation: from greeting to 'yes'
objectives: Lead a selling conversation in five clear stages
Turn product features into customer benefits
State your price clearly without apologising
Ask for the sale and arrange payment and delivery

blocks.text: A good price only becomes money when someone buys. Selling is not about pressure or clever tricks. It is a short, friendly conversation in which you find out what the customer needs, show how your product meets that need, state your price clearly and make it easy to say yes. The same stages work face to face in the market, on the phone and on WhatsApp.

blocks.title: Five stages of a sale
items: Greet and connect
Ask about needs
Show benefits
State the price
Ask for the sale
blocks.caption: Most lost sales skip stage 2 or stage 5: sellers talk before listening, or never actually ask the customer to buy.

blocks.text: Stage 1: greet and connect

Greet warmly and use the customer's name if you know it. In person, smile and give your full attention; put the phone down. On WhatsApp, reply as quickly as you can, because a buyer who waits a long time often buys elsewhere. A short, polite opening is enough: 'Good afternoon, Mrs Bello. Thank you for your message. How can I help you today?'
Stage 2: ask before you tell

Ask two or three simple questions to understand what she wants. **Who is it for? When does she need it? What matters most to her: size, taste, style, speed or price?** Her answers tell you which product to suggest and which benefits to talk about. A customer buying chin chin for a child's birthday party cares about quantity and delivery time; one buying a gift cares about packaging.
Stage 3: show benefits, not just features
A **feature** is a fact about the product. A **benefit** is what that fact does for the customer. Customers buy benefits. Always link the two with the words 'which means'.

head: Feature
Benefit (which means...)
rows: Fried fresh on the morning of delivery
It is crunchy and tastes homemade when your guests eat it
It stays fresh for days and looks neat as a gift
Gown finished in 3 days with one free adjustment
You will be ready for Saturday's wedding and it will fit perfectly
You do not need to leave work or pay for transport

blocks.name: business-chat
blocks.alt: Two people talking about a product
blocks.caption: Listening first lets you talk about the benefits that matter to this customer.

blocks.text: Stage 4: state the price clearly

Say the price plainly, with the benefit next to it, then stop talking. 'The 200 gram pack is ₦800, fried fresh and delivered to your office.' Do not add 'I know it is a bit much' or 'but I can reduce'. Apologising tells the buyer you do not believe in your own price, and invites bargaining. A short silence after the price is normal; let the customer think.

blocks.title: Practise your price out loud
blocks.text: Say your price and one benefit ten times in front of a mirror or to a friend, until it sounds calm and normal. Many sellers find their voice shakes the first few times. Practice is the cure.
Stage 5: ask for the sale

When the customer seems interested, ask a simple closing question that moves things forward: 'How many packs would you like?', 'Shall I deliver on Thursday or Friday?' or 'Would you like to pay by transfer or cash on delivery?' These questions assume the sale politely and make the next step easy. Then confirm the details: item, quantity, price, total, payment method, delivery day and address.

blocks.title: Worked example: a WhatsApp enquiry
blocks.context: For example, Funmi asks Ngozi on WhatsApp: 'How much is your chin chin?' Figures are approximate.
steps: Greet: 'Good morning Funmi, thank you for asking!'
Ask: 'Is it for yourself, an office, or an event? When do you need it?' Funmi says it is for a birthday party of about 25 children on Saturday.
Benefit: 'For a party, the 200 g packs work well. Each child gets their own sealed pack, fried fresh on Friday.'
Price: '₦800 per pack. For 25 packs that is ₦20,000, delivered to you on Saturday morning.'
Close: 'Would you like me to book 25 packs for you? I take a 50% deposit (₦10,000) to confirm, and the balance on delivery.'
blocks.result: Funmi pays the deposit. Ngozi checks her bank app, sees the ₦10,000, and sends a written confirmation of the order.

blocks.text: After the sale

items: Thank the customer and confirm the order in writing (a WhatsApp message is fine).
Deliver exactly what you promised, on time. If there is a delay, tell her early.
Follow up a day later: 'Did the children enjoy it?' This builds trust and often brings the next order.
Ask happy customers if you can share their kind words, and save their number for future offers.

blocks.text: If you use the free WhatsApp Business app, you can set up a short catalogue with photos and prices, quick replies for common questions and labels to track new orders and paid orders. These features save time, but the five stages above still do the selling.

takeaways: Selling is a conversation: greet, ask, show benefits, state price, ask for the sale.
Ask about needs before describing the product.
Link features to benefits with 'which means'.
State the price with a benefit, then stop talking.
Confirm orders in writing and follow up after delivery.

activity.title: Script and practise one sale
steps: Write a five-stage script for your product: greeting, two questions, three benefits, price sentence, closing question.
Turn three features of your product into benefits using 'which means'.
Practise saying your price sentence out loud ten times.
Role-play the whole conversation with a friend or family member.
Ask them which part sounded least confident and practise that part again.
activity.evidence: Your written script, plus a short voice note or note of the role-play and the feedback you received.

lessons.title: Handling price objections and bargaining honestly
objectives: Respond to 'it is too expensive' using a four-step method
Bargain with a planned starting price and walk-away price
Handle 'I will think about it' and 'another seller is cheaper'
Apply honest, fair selling practices

blocks.text: An **objection** is a reason a customer gives for not buying yet. Objections are normal and often a good sign: a customer who objects is still interested enough to talk. Most objections are about price, trust or timing. The goal is not to win an argument but to understand the real concern and answer it honestly.
A four-step method for any objection

blocks.title: Respond to an objection
items: Listen fully
Acknowledge the concern
Ask a clarifying question
Respond with value or options
blocks.caption: After responding, check if the concern is settled; if not, go round again calmly.

items: **Listen** to the whole objection without interrupting or defending yourself.
**Acknowledge** it respectfully: 'I understand, you want to be sure it is worth the money.'
**Ask** a question to find the real concern: 'Is it the total amount, or are you comparing with another seller?'
**Respond** with value, a different option, or honest facts. Then check: 'Does that help?'

blocks.text: Common objections and good responses

head: The customer says
What it may really mean
A good response
rows: I do not yet see why it costs this much, or my budget is smaller
Explain the benefits again, or offer a smaller size or quantity that fits her budget, rather than cutting the price
I am not sure your product is different
Ask what she is comparing; show the difference in size, freshness, finish or delivery
I have a doubt I have not said
Ask kindly what she is unsure about; offer to hold the item until a set time
Hold the price with a reason, or offer value (delivery, a free extra) instead of a cut
I do not trust online sellers
I fear paying and getting nothing
Offer pay on delivery for nearby orders, share real reviews, show your business details

blocks.name: handshake
blocks.caption: An objection handled with respect often ends in a deal and a returning customer.

blocks.text: Notice that none of the good responses starts with a price cut. When you reduce the price at the first sign of hesitation, you lose profit and you also suggest that your first price was not honest. Offering a smaller size, a different style or a payment plan keeps your price per item intact while still helping the customer who truly has a smaller budget.
Bargaining in the market

In many Nigerian markets, buyers expect to bargain, and refusing completely can seem unfriendly. The answer is to plan. For each item, decide three numbers in advance: your **asking price**, your **target price** and your **walk-away price**. The walk-away price must be above your true cost. Start at the asking price, move slowly and in small steps, and give something only when you get something, such as a bigger quantity or immediate payment.

blocks.title: Worked example: bargaining over a gown
blocks.context: For example, a customer asks Amaka to sew a gown. Amaka's true cost is ₦11,000. Her plan: asking ₦18,000, target ₦17,000, walk-away ₦15,000. Figures are approximate.
steps: Amaka listens and acknowledges: 'I understand you want a good price.' She asks: 'When do you need it?' The customer needs it for a wedding in 4 days.
Amaka responds with value: 'I will fit you on Wednesday and deliver on Friday, with one free adjustment. Many tailors will not finish in time.'
Customer: 'Make it ₦15,000.' Amaka offers ₦17,000 if paid in full today.
They agree at ₦17,000 with full payment, which Amaka confirms in her bank app.
blocks.result: Profit is ₦17,000 − ₦11,000 = ₦6,000, a 35% margin. Amaka stayed above her walk-away price and gave a reason for every move.

blocks.title: Do not split the difference by reflex
blocks.text: If the customer offers half your price and you meet in the middle each time, you will end up far below your plan. Move in small steps, and only in exchange for something, such as full payment, a bigger order or collection instead of delivery.
Selling honestly

items: Describe your product truthfully. Do not claim it 'cures', 'whitens' or 'lasts forever' if you cannot prove it.
Give the full weight, quantity or size you advertise, and use accurate scales.
Treat customers fairly: the same item should carry the same price for similar customers on the same terms.
Be honest about delivery time. Promise what you can do, then do it.
If something goes wrong, admit it and fix it quickly: replace, refund or repair.

blocks.text: Honesty is also good business. Word of mouth and WhatsApp status travel fast; one unhappy customer who feels cheated can cost you many sales. Nigeria also has a federal consumer protection agency, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC), which handles consumer complaints, another reason to deal fairly.

blocks.title: It is fine to lose some sales
blocks.text: Not every buyer is your customer. If someone only wants a price below your cost, wish her well. Losing a sale that would have lost you money is a win.

takeaways: Objections are normal and show interest.
Listen, acknowledge, ask, then respond.
Offer a smaller option or extra value before cutting price.
Plan asking, target and walk-away prices; never go below cost.
Sell honestly: true claims, full quantity, fair prices, realistic promises.

activity.title: Prepare for objections
steps: Write the three objections you hear most often.
For each, write what it may really mean and your four-step response.
Set asking, target and walk-away prices for your main product.
Role-play bargaining with a friend who pushes hard on price.
Note what you gave up and what you got in return.
activity.evidence: An objection sheet with your three objections and responses, plus your three planned prices for one item.

lessons.title: Recording daily sales and tracking your profit
objectives: Keep a daily sales book with the right columns
Calculate daily and weekly revenue, gross profit and margin
Work out a simple break-even number for fixed costs
Use your records to spot problems early

blocks.text: Records turn guesses into facts. With a few minutes each evening, you can know exactly what you sold, how much profit you made, which products earn the most and whether your margin is holding. Without records, it is easy to feel busy and still be losing money.
Your daily sales book
Use a notebook or a phone spreadsheet with one line for each sale or each item type per day. These columns are enough for most small businesses:

**Sales amount** = quantity × price. **Profit** here means gross profit: sales amount minus quantity × true cost. Because your true cost already includes your wage and an overhead share, this profit is what the business truly earned. In the example, Monday's margin is ₦11,100 ÷ ₦35,700 = 31%.

blocks.name: receipt
blocks.alt: A receipt with a list of items and a total
blocks.caption: Writing every sale down each day shows your real profit, not just money in hand.

blocks.text: A weekly summary
Every week, add up your daily pages and write a short summary. Five numbers tell you most of what you need to know:

items: **Total sales (revenue):** all money from sales this week.
**Total gross profit:** sales minus the true cost of the items sold.
**Margin:** gross profit ÷ sales. Compare it with the margin you planned. If it is falling, find out why.
**Discounts given:** total naira given away in discounts and bargaining.
**Best and slowest items:** which products sold most and which barely moved.

blocks.title: Your record rhythm
items: Each sale: write it down
Each evening: total the day
Each week: five-number summary
Each month: compare and review
blocks.caption: Small, regular steps keep records accurate without taking much time.

blocks.text: Break-even: how much must you sell?

Some costs are fixed: they stay the same no matter how much you sell, such as monthly shop rent, a market levy or a staff salary. Your **break-even point** is the number of items you must sell to cover those fixed costs. The formula is: fixed costs ÷ profit per item (price minus the cost of making one item).

blocks.title: Worked example: should Ngozi rent a kiosk?
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi is offered a small kiosk near an office complex for about ₦30,000 a month. She currently sells from home. Figures are approximate.
steps: Her profit per pack (price ₦800 minus true cost ₦550) is ₦250.
Break-even: ₦30,000 ÷ ₦250 = 120 packs a month just to pay the kiosk rent.
That is about 5 extra packs a day over 24 trading days.
Her records show walk-in buyers at a similar spot bought about 10 packs a day when she tested a table there for a week.
Expected extra profit: (10 − 5) × ₦250 × 24 days = ₦30,000 a month after rent.
blocks.result: Because her records gave her a real number for daily sales, Ngozi can decide using facts, not hope. She takes the kiosk and checks after one month whether sales match the test.

blocks.text: Two more numbers worth tracking

**Enquiries versus sales.** Keep a simple tally of how many people ask about your product (in person, by phone or on WhatsApp) and how many actually buy. If 20 people ask in a week and 4 buy, 1 in 5 enquiries becomes a sale. If many people ask but few buy, look at your selling conversation, your photos or how you state the price. If few people ask at all, the problem is more likely visibility than price.

**Repeat customers.** Put a small mark next to the name of anyone who buys again. Repeat buyers are the cheapest sales you will ever make, because you do not have to find them again. If your repeat customers keep coming back after a price rise, that is strong evidence your price is fair.

At the end of each day, also count the cash in your bag and compare it with the cash sales you wrote down, and check that transfers in your app match the transfer sales in your book. If the numbers do not agree, find the gap that same day while you still remember the sales.

blocks.title: Watch your margin, not just your sales
blocks.text: Sales can rise while profit falls, for example when input prices go up but your price stays the same, or when you give more discounts. A falling margin in your weekly summary is your early warning to recalculate costs.

blocks.title: Use what you already have
blocks.text: If customers pay by transfer, your bank or wallet app keeps a history you can check against your sales book. Many POS and payment providers also show daily totals. Cash sales still need writing down, because they leave no trail.

takeaways: Write every sale: item, quantity, price, amount, cost, profit, payment type.
Margin = gross profit ÷ sales; compare it with your plan every week.
Track discounts and best and slowest items.
Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ profit per item.
A falling margin is a signal to recalculate costs and prices.

activity.title: Start your sales book
steps: Draw the eight sales book columns in your notebook or phone sheet.
Record every sale for seven days.
Total each day and calculate the day's margin.
At the end of the week, write your five-number summary.
Calculate the break-even number for one fixed cost you pay or are considering.
activity.evidence: Seven days of sales records and a weekly summary page, photographed or saved.

quiz.q: A customer asks 'How much is it?' on WhatsApp. According to the five stages, what should Ngozi usually do before giving a long description?
options: Ask a question about who it is for and when it is needed
Wait a day to seem busy
quiz.explain: Asking about needs first lets her talk about the benefits that matter and suggest the right product.

quiz.q: Which sentence turns a feature into a benefit?
options: Delivered to your office, which means you do not lose work time
quiz.explain: A benefit explains what the feature does for the customer, often linked with 'which means'.

quiz.q: Amaka's true cost is ₦11,000 and her walk-away price is ₦15,000. A customer insists on ₦12,000 and will not move. What should she do?
options: Accept to avoid losing the sale
Accept and use cheaper lining without telling her
Politely decline or offer a simpler style that fits the budget above her floor
Ask for the money first and decide later
quiz.explain: ₦12,000 is below her walk-away price. Offering a simpler option or declining protects her profit and honesty.

quiz.q: A day's sales are ₦40,000 and the true cost of the items sold is ₦28,000. What is the margin?
Shop rent is ₦45,000 a month and profit per item is ₦300. What is the break-even number of items per month?
quiz.explain: Break-even = fixed costs ÷ profit per item = ₦45,000 ÷ ₦300 = 150 items.

quiz.q: A customer says 'I will think about it.' What is the best next step?
options: Kindly ask what she is unsure about and offer to hold the item until a set time
Tell her the price will double tomorrow
quiz.explain: 'I will think about it' often hides an unspoken doubt. A gentle question uncovers it without pressure or false urgency.

modules.title: Portfolio and impact: your price, your plan
modules.overview: Bring your work together into a one-page pricing sheet, present your price and value clearly, including when prices must rise, and write a 90-day review plan. These three pieces form your capstone project.

lessons.title: Building your one-page pricing sheet
objectives: Assemble cost, market and value evidence on one page
Choose and justify a final price with its margin
Set bulk, discount and walk-away prices that stay above cost
Check your sheet for common errors before using it

blocks.text: This lesson pulls together everything you have done so far into a single **pricing sheet** for your chosen product or service. It is the main part of your capstone project. A good pricing sheet lets anyone, including you six months from now, see exactly how your price was set and why. Keep it in your notebook or as one tab in a phone spreadsheet.
The six parts of a pricing sheet

blocks.title: Pricing sheet contents
items: True cost per item
Market range per unit
Value points
Chosen price and margin
Offer and walk-away prices
Date and next review
blocks.caption: If any part is missing, your price is partly a guess.

items: **True cost.** Copy your cost sheet from Module 1: direct costs, labour, overhead share, waste, and the final cost per item.
**Market range.** From your survey in Module 2, write the lowest, middle and highest price per unit you found.
**Value points.** List the two or three benefits customers told you they value most.
**Chosen price.** Write your standard price, the profit per item, the markup and the margin.
**Offers and limits.** Write your bulk price, any planned promotion, and your walk-away price, each with its profit per item.
**Dates.** Write the date you made the sheet and the date you will next review it.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi's finished pricing sheet
blocks.context: For example, this is Ngozi's sheet for her 200 g chin chin pack. All figures are approximate and for illustration.
steps: True cost: direct ₦375 (ingredients and gas ₦325, packaging ₦50), labour ₦125, overhead ₦50. Total ₦550 per pack.
Market range: ₦360 to ₦600 per 100 g. Her ₦800 for 200 g is ₦400 per 100 g, lower middle.
Value points: fried fresh on delivery day, delivered to offices, sealed and labelled.
Standard price ₦800: profit ₦250, markup 45%, margin 31%.
Bulk (30+ packs, one delivery): ₦750, true cost ₦520, profit ₦230, margin 31%. Walk-away price: ₦650, profit ₦100.
Made on 6 October; next review in 30 days, or sooner if flour or oil prices move.
blocks.result: Every number on the sheet can be traced back to a receipt, a timed batch, a market survey or a customer's words. That is what makes her price defensible.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.caption: Your pricing sheet is the evidence behind every price you quote.

blocks.text: Choosing your final price

Look at your cost-plus price, your market range and your value points together. Then choose a price and write one or two sentences explaining it. For example: 'I chose ₦800 because it gives me a 31% margin after paying myself, sits in the lower middle of the market, and my office customers value fresh delivery.' If you cannot write that sentence, go back and fill the gap.

head: Situation
What it suggests
rows: Cost-plus price is below the market range
You may be undercharging; consider moving up toward the middle
Cost-plus price is inside the range
Good position; use value points to decide low, middle or high
Cost-plus price is above the whole range
Reduce costs, offer a smaller size, or clearly add value
You may have room for a small increase; test it carefully

blocks.title: Common errors to check
blocks.text: Did you divide by good items, not total items? Did you include your labour and overhead? Did you use margin and markup correctly? Is your walk-away price above your true cost? Are your input prices from the last month, not last year?

Keep your old price on the sheet too, crossed out but readable, with a short note of what changed. If you moved from ₦500 to ₦800, write why: labour now counted, overhead included, market checked. This before-and-after comparison is strong evidence of what you learned, and it reminds you never to slip back into guessing.
If you sell more than one product

Make one sheet for your main product first. Then repeat the cost calculation for each other item, because different items carry different costs and margins. You may find that one item you thought was popular earns very little, while a quieter item is your best earner. That knowledge helps you decide what to promote and what to reprice or drop.

If you sell a service, do the same with one standard job. You can also set an hourly or daily rate: true cost per hour (your hourly labour rate plus overhead per hour), divided by one minus your target margin. For example, ₦1,000 labour plus ₦250 overhead is ₦1,250 per hour; for a 35% margin, ₦1,250 ÷ 0.65 = about ₦1,920, so roughly ₦2,000 an hour.

blocks.title: Show your sheet to someone honest
blocks.text: Ask a trusted person, such as a fellow trader or a WODDI group member, to check your sheet. Fresh eyes often spot a missing cost or a price that is too modest.

takeaways: One page holds cost, market, value, price, offers and dates.
Write a sentence explaining why you chose your price.
Every offer and walk-away price must show its profit and stay above cost.
Check divisions, labour, overhead, formulas and date of input prices.
Make a separate sheet for each product or standard service.

steps: Copy your true cost from your Module 1 cost sheet.
Add your market range and value points from Module 2.
Write your chosen price, profit, markup, margin and one sentence of reasoning.
Add bulk, promotion and walk-away prices with their profit.

lessons.title: Communicating your price and value with confidence
objectives: Write a clear price list and product description
Present prices on WhatsApp and in person without apology
Announce a price increase respectfully
Explain your pricing method to another trader or employer

blocks.text: Customers judge your price partly by how you present it. A neat, clear price list with real benefits makes a fair price feel fair. Vague answers, prices that change from person to person, and nervous apologies make even a low price feel suspicious. This lesson helps you present your price in writing, in person, and when it has to go up.
A clear price list

Write your prices down and share the same list with everyone. For each item, include the name, size or quantity, price, and one short benefit. Add how to order, how to pay and delivery terms. Print it, pin it to your stall, or save it as an image you can send on WhatsApp in one tap.

head: Item
Size
Price (approx.)
Why customers choose it
rows: Sealed and labelled, great as a gift
Booked with 50% deposit, delivered on the day

blocks.title: Show the price
blocks.text: Many online sellers answer 'DM for price'. Some buyers find this frustrating and move on. Showing your price openly saves time for both of you and attracts customers who are happy with it.

blocks.name: mobile-marketing
blocks.alt: A woman sharing products on her phone
blocks.caption: A clear price list on WhatsApp answers the first question before it is asked.

blocks.text: Your product description matters as much as the number. Use clear photos taken in daylight against a plain background, and write a short description that names the size, the main benefit and how to order. For example: '200 g chin chin, fried fresh on delivery day. Sealed and labelled. ₦800. Order by Wednesday for Friday delivery to offices in Independence Layout.' One specific line like this answers most questions before they are asked and makes your price look considered.

Keep your prices consistent across every channel. If your stall says ₦800 and your WhatsApp catalogue says ₦750, customers will notice and will start to ask for the lower price everywhere. Update every list on the same day whenever you change a price.
Saying it in person

Use the price sentence from Module 3: price plus one benefit, then silence. Stand or sit upright, look at the customer and speak at a normal pace. If you feel nervous, slow down. Remember that your price is not a personal favour or a guess; it is a calculated figure on your pricing sheet. You are simply telling the customer what it is.
When your price has to go up
Input prices change, and sometimes your price must change too. Handled well, most regular customers accept it. Handled badly, they feel ambushed.

blocks.title: Announcing a price increase
items: Recalculate and decide
Tell regulars early
Honour existing orders
New price starts
Check sales after
blocks.caption: Giving notice and honouring orders already agreed keeps trust while you protect your margin.

blocks.title: Worked example: a respectful price increase message
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi's flour and oil costs rise and her true cost goes from ₦550 to ₦600 a pack. Her margin at ₦800 falls to 25%. Figures are approximate.
steps: She calculates: for a 30% margin, ₦600 ÷ 0.70 = ₦857. She chooses ₦850.

Two weeks ahead she sends her regulars a WhatsApp message: 'Dear valued customer, thank you for your support. Because flour and oil prices have risen, from 1 November the 200 g pack will be ₦850. Orders placed before then stay at ₦800. I will keep frying fresh and delivering on time.'
She honours every order placed before the date at the old price.
From 1 November she updates her price list and catalogue.
She tracks sales for four weeks in her sales book.
blocks.result: Her new margin is ₦250 ÷ ₦850 = 29%. Most regulars stay because the message was early, honest and short.

blocks.title: Other options besides a higher price
blocks.text: If you fear customers will not accept a higher price, you can offer a slightly smaller pack at the old price alongside the standard pack at the new price. Be open about the size; reducing the quantity quietly without telling customers damages trust.
Explaining your method to others

Being able to explain how you price is a valuable skill for a job interview, a loan or grant application, or helping a fellow trader. Be specific: 'I calculate my true cost including materials, my labour and overhead, check five competitors per 100 g, then set a price with about a 30% margin. When I did this, I found I had been selling below cost.' Real numbers from your own pricing sheet are far more convincing than general claims. Be honest too: pricing is a skill you keep improving with practice and records, not something you master once.

takeaways: Share one clear price list with everyone.
Include size, price, benefit, ordering, payment and delivery terms.
State your price calmly; it is a calculated figure, not a guess.
Give notice of increases and honour existing orders.
Explain your method with your own real numbers.

activity.title: Create your price list and value message
steps: Design a price list for your products with size, price and one benefit each.
Save it as an image or print it.
Write a short, respectful price-increase message you could use in future.
Write a three-sentence explanation of how you set your price.
Share the price list with three customers and note their reactions.

lessons.title: Your 90-day pricing review plan and next steps
objectives: Set review dates and triggers for repricing
Use your sales records to judge whether a price is working
Write a 90-day plan with specific actions
Check your capstone evidence before the final quiz

blocks.text: A price is not set once and forgotten. Costs change, your skill and reputation grow, and customers' needs shift. This final lesson helps you build a 90-day plan so that reviewing your price becomes a routine, not a crisis. It also walks you through checking your capstone evidence before you take the final quiz.
When to review your price

items: **On a fixed schedule:** for example, at the end of every month, using your weekly summaries.
**When a major input price moves:** if the price of a main ingredient, material or transport changes noticeably, recalculate that week.
**When your margin falls:** if your weekly margin drops a few points below your plan for two or three weeks.
**When demand changes:** if you are always sold out (you may be underpriced) or sales slow sharply (check price, quality and visibility).

blocks.title: The pricing review loop
items: Record sales and costs
Review margin monthly
Recalculate true cost
Adjust price or offer
Communicate the change
blocks.caption: Each 30-day loop keeps your price matched to your real costs and market.

blocks.text: Reading your records

At each review, look at four things side by side: your current true cost, your margin for the month, the number of items sold, and the discounts you gave. A healthy picture is a steady or rising margin with steady sales. If margin is falling while sales are steady, costs have probably risen. If sales fall after a price rise, check whether the fall is larger than the extra-sales rule says you can afford (Module 2, Lesson 3) before deciding to reverse it.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi's first 90 days
blocks.context: For example, this is how Ngozi uses the review loop over three months. Figures are approximate.
steps: Month 1: sells 220 packs at ₦800. True cost ₦550. Margin 31%, as planned. She notes that office bulk orders are her steadiest sales.
Month 2: flour and oil rise; true cost becomes ₦600. Margin falls to 25%. She gives two weeks' notice and moves to ₦850.
Month 3: sells 205 packs at ₦850. Profit per pack ₦250, total ₦51,250, compared with ₦55,000 in Month 1 and only ₦44,000 if she had stayed at ₦800 on 220 packs.
She also notices the 100 g pack has a lower margin and sells slowly, so she plans to review its price next month.
blocks.result: Without the review, Month 3 profit at the old price would have been lower even with more sales. With it, her margin is back to 29% and she has a clear next step.

blocks.text: Do not change your price every week. Frequent small changes confuse customers and make it hard to tell what is working. Unless a cost rises sharply, keep a price for at least a month, collect the records, and then decide. One clear change backed by numbers is better than many nervous adjustments.
Writing your 90-day plan

head: When
Action
Evidence
rows: Start using the new price and price list
Record every sale; weekly five-number summary
First review: recalc cost, check margin and sales
Second review; test one offer (bulk or bundle)
Full review; decide next price and next product to price

blocks.name: calendar
blocks.caption: Put your review dates in your phone calendar so they are not forgotten.

blocks.text: Check your capstone evidence

Your capstone has three parts. First, a **calculated true cost and considered price** with a genuine margin for a real product or service: your pricing sheet from Lesson 1. Second, **documentation of a real or practised selling conversation** using this price: your script, a note of what was said, or a short voice note, with what you learned. Third, this **90-day review plan**. Your certificate should reflect a price you actually calculated, not one you guessed.

blocks.title: Be honest in your reflection
blocks.text: If your first selling conversation did not go well, say so and explain what you would change. Honest reflection shows real learning far better than a perfect-sounding story.
Where to go next

items: Price your second product using the same sheet.
Explore basic bookkeeping so you can produce a monthly profit and loss summary.
If you sell food, cosmetics or similar regulated products, find out from NAFDAC whether your product needs registration before you scale up.
If your business is growing, consider registering a business name with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) and opening a business account in that name.

blocks.title: Celebrate the shift
blocks.text: You started this course with a price that may have been a guess. You now have a calculated floor, a market view, a value story, a selling script and a review plan. That is a real business skill.

takeaways: Review prices monthly and whenever key costs move.
Watch margin, sales, true cost and discounts together.
Use the extra-sales rule before reversing a price rise.
Write a 90-day plan with dated actions and evidence.
Capstone: pricing sheet, selling conversation, 90-day plan.
